Two sentences later (ch5:1031-1034) the thesis's own rule runs canMatch "on every level it matches" and canActivateChild "on the levels above an entered one", both of which include kept levels. Re-running also depends on runGuardsAndResolvers and on RouteReuseStrategy. mifos sets runGuardsAndResolvers to 'always' (accounting-routing.module.ts:219,262,305; system-routing.module.ts:374), to 'pathParamsOrQueryParamsChange' (products-routing.module.ts:325-360) and to 'paramsOrQueryParamsChange' (search-routing.module.ts:29). It also provides a custom RouteReuseStrategy (core/route/route-reusable-strategy.ts, core.module.ts:115).
consequence: A general claim about Angular in the abstract is wrong for two guard kinds and conditional on configuration that a corpus application changes. A reader would take it as framework behaviour.
fix: Abstract: "...between screens under one parent whose canActivate guard the router does not run again (it re-runs canMatch, and canActivateChild when a child is entered)". ch5:1027: "Angular does not run a kept route's canActivate or resolvers again unless its parameters change or runGuardsAndResolvers asks; canMatch and an ancestor's canActivateChild do run again."

verdict.reasoning:
Only part of the finding holds. The real defect is ch5-results.tex:1027-1030. The rest is either wrong or does not apply.

What holds: ch5:1027 says "Angular does not run a guard again on a route a navigation keeps, so a navigation between two children of a guarded parent runs the children's guards and not the parent's". As a statement about Angular, that is false for two guard kinds. canMatch runs during route matching on every navigation, kept routes included. A kept parent's canActivateChild runs whenever a child is entered. The paragraph's own next sentence (ch5:1031-1034) and the extractor's rule both say so: extract.ts:206-209 runs `t.flatMap((l) => l.canMatch)` over every level and `t.slice(0, -1).flatMap((l) => l.canActivateChild)` whenever anything is entered. So the paragraph contradicts itself. ch3-analysis.tex:152-154 and the docstring at routes.ts:91-94 already state the claim correctly, limited to canActivate and resolvers. ch5 is the outlier. It is the same claim as PDF text lines 3745-3747.

What does not hold:
(1) RouteReuseStrategy. In Angular 18.2.14 the guard check (router.mjs:3234, getRouteGuards) decides whether to run guards again from `future.routeConfig === curr.routeConfig` and runGuardsAndResolvers only. It never consults RouteReuseStrategy. mifos's strategy (src/app/core/route/route-reusable-strategy.ts) also returns `future.routeConfig === curr.routeConfig || future.data.reuse`, which only widens reuse of components. The objection has no basis.
(2) runGuardsAndResolvers. ch5:1034-1035 defines a kept level to exclude one whose parameter can change or that "ask[s] to run its guards on every navigation". The code (routes.ts:117, `always: run !== undefined && runMode !== 'paramsChange' && runMode !== 'pathParamsChange'`) treats 'always', 'pathParamsOrQueryParamsChange' and 'paramsOrQueryParamsChange' as not kept. So the mifos settings cannot produce a wrong must edge, and the prose's "kept" already excludes them.
(3) The abstract (thesis.tex:164-165, 119-120) is not a general claim about Angular. It describes the must-tier edges. Under this rule, a must edge between children of a shared parent exists only if the parent has no canMatch and no canActivateChild, and no runGuardsAndResolvers outside paramsChange/pathParamsChange (a parameter in the parent's path also stops it being kept). So "the router does not guard again" is true of those edges by construction.

Severity is minor, not major: one sentence in ch5 is imprecise and contradicted two lines later. No number, rule or measured result changes.

title: "Source-behind" counts guards by name, but factory guards print without arguments
evidence: ch5:1098-1101: for \GuardOnlySourceBehind=37 of \GuardOnlyGuarded=41 edges, every guard "is one the source screen's own routes carry by name ... so a user on that screen has passed it once already". guard-only.mjs passed() compares guard text. adapter-angular/src/guards.ts writes any factory call as `${callee}()` and drops its arguments, which ch4:488-489 concedes. bitwarden/apps/web has 27 organizationPermissionsGuard(...) calls with different predicates, e.g. organizationPermissionsGuard(canAccessOrgAdmin) at organization-routing.module.ts:27 and organizationPermissionsGuard((o) => o.isOwner) at settings/organization-settings-routing.module.ts:28. All of them print the same. ch6:609 says a guard is identified "by the text of its expression", which is not true for factories.
consequence: Some of bitwarden's 7 source-behind edges may need a different predicate than the one the user passed. "Has passed it once already" is then false. Passing a state-dependent guard once does not mean it will pass again in any case.
fix: ch5:1098-1101: "...one the source screen's routes carry under the same printed name. A guard factory is printed without its arguments, so two factories with different predicates count as one; the count is an upper bound." Delete "so the user has passed it once already" in ch7:154. Correct ch6:609 to say factories are identified by their callee alone.

verdict.reasoning:
The mechanism the finding describes is real, but it does not reach the counted edges, so the count is not inflated and the overclaim does not hold.

The mechanism: packages/adapter-angular/src/guards.ts:114-116 prints a call-expression guard as `${callee}()` and drops its arguments. guard-only.mjs:20-24 passed() compares those printed texts. ch4-evaluation.tex:490 already admits the arguments are dropped.

The data: I re-ran guard-only's logic on the current corpus with the same imports and the UIGRAPH_IGNORE_GUARDS=1 path, and listed every guarded must edge. The 37 source-behind edges (\GuardOnlySourceBehind=37 of \GuardOnlyGuarded=41, matching results-must/guard-only.json) break down as follows:
- ghostfolio, 29 edges: the guard is `AuthGuard`, a class reference with no arguments.
- alfresco, 1 edge (n_profile->n_personal-files): the guard is `AuthGuard`.
- bitwarden, 7 edges: all go to n_login and the guard is `unauthGuardFn()`. The sources are verify-recover-delete-org, login-with-passkey, sso-login-failed, authentication-timeout, recover-2fa, recover-delete and verify-recover-delete.

Every one of the 18 `unauthGuardFn(` call sites in bitwarden is written with no arguments (apps/web/src/app/oss-routing.module.ts:152, 163, 185, 210, 243, 251, 256, 317, 377, 396, 422, 461, 483, 505, 545, 567, 608, 620). So the printed text and the real guard expression are the same, and the guard the user passed on the source route really is the guard the navigation runs.

The finding's example, organizationPermissionsGuard(...), is on none of bitwarden's 8 guarded must edges. The eighth edge, premium_checkout_success->settings_subscription_premium, is guarded by `isSelfHosted,deepLinkGuard(),authGuard` and was already not counted as source-behind. So no factory with arguments is in the 37, and the "upper bound" caveat would describe a case that does not occur.

The second consequence also misreads the prose. ch5:1100-1101 and ch7:154 say only that the user "has passed it once already", which is literally true for identical guards. They do not claim the guard will pass again.

What is left is a minor wording slip, not an overclaim. ch6-discussion.tex:609 says "A guard is identified by the text of its expression". For a factory call with arguments that is inaccurate: only the callee is kept. The sentence also names only the opposite risk, that two equivalent guards count as two. That limitation is real, but it does not touch any reported number here.

title: RQ3 claims no must-tier precision cost, but the evidence cannot test it
evidence: ch5:587: "Scope attribution therefore raises coverage without lowering must-tier precision". ch5:608: it "adds no deterministic transition the evidence does not support". ch5:467-468: "attribution costs the deterministic tier nothing". Attribution takes the tier from \CensusBaseMust=17 to \CensusMust=150, k8sdash from 0 to 125. The only checks on those edges are the witness check, which ch3:145-146 says "does not establish" the claim, and the non-independent tier reading (ch5:1089-1091). ch5:260 itself says "the tier is too small for that to be a precision figure".
consequence: The RQ3 answer asserts a precision property the thesis says elsewhere it cannot measure, for 133 added must edges.
fix: Replace ch5:587-588 with: "Scope attribution raises coverage and adds \CensusMust{}$-$\CensusBaseMust{} must edges without a witness-check failure; whether they occur on every input rests on the demotion rules and is not independently verified." Make the same change at ch5:608 and ch5:467-468.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding rests on treating "must-tier precision" as the soundness property in Claim~\ref{claim:must}. The thesis does not use the term that way. ch4-evaluation.tex:261-265 defines must-tier precision operationally: the fraction of must edges whose witness line holds a construct of the claimed kind with the claimed target, and whose destination sits at an address the independent route set declares. ch4-evaluation.tex:273 then sets the RQ3 test as "coverage rises and must-tier precision does not fall". Table tab:methods (ch4:314) lists the witness check as the method that measures exactly this quantity. So the claim that the evidence "cannot test it" is false. The check measures it, and generated-must-witness.tex gives \MustWitnessEdges=150 and \MustWitnessViolations=0, so the defined metric is 100% after attribution. It cannot have fallen.

The finding's citation of ch3:145-146 ("agreement does not establish it") is about Claim~\ref{claim:must} (soundness on every input), not about precision. Mixing up the two is the error.

The cited sentences are also hedged in place. ch5:589-611, the same paragraph as 587, gives three qualifications. It says a too-wide scope "produces edges whose witnesses all pass ... so no witness-based method can find it" (ch5:604-606), and that "the scopes are not too large is not established" (ch5:610-611). ch5:608 limits itself to what "the evidence" supports. ch5:467-468 says the "costs nothing" result "is only meaningful because the attribution is narrow", then says at once that on this corpus "it is not very narrow".

What is left is a minor wording tension, and it points the other way. ch5:260 says "the tier is too small for that to be a precision figure", which undersells a quantity ch4 defines as precision. ch7-conclusion.tex:45-46 phrases it better: "too small for that to be a statement about precision in general". The proposed fix would weaken a sentence that is correct under the thesis's own definition, and leave the actually inconsistent line, ch5:260, as it is.
verdict.checkedEvidence:
- ch4-evaluation.tex:256-273: the RQ3 metric definition. "Must-tier precision is the fraction of must edges whose witness line contains a construct of the claimed kind with the claimed target, and whose destination node sits at an address the independent route set declares"; "RQ3 is answered positively only if coverage rises and must-tier precision does not fall".
- ch4-evaluation.tex:314: tab:methods maps "Witness check" to "Must-tier precision".
- generated-must-witness.tex:3-4: \MustWitnessEdges=150, \MustWitnessViolations=0.
- generated-census.tex:26 and :44: \CensusMust=150 and \CensusMustKdash=125.
- generated-census-base.tex:26: \CensusBaseMust=17.
- generated-before-after.tex:59-60: \AttrMustBefore=18, \AttrMustAfter=20.
- ch3:139-146: the "does not establish" wording refers to Claim~\ref{claim:must} (soundness), not to precision.
- ch5:587-611: qualifications in the same paragraph, including "no witness-based method can find it" (606) and "not established" (611).
- ch5:464-473: "only meaningful because the attribution is narrow ... on this corpus it is not very narrow".
- ch5:255-260: the actual internal tension, "too small for that to be a precision figure".
- ch7:45-46: the softer "statement about precision in general".
verdict.betterFix: Do not change ch5:587, 608 or 467-468. They match the RQ3 criterion defined at ch4:261-273, and their own paragraphs already carry the too-wide-scope caveat. Optionally, to remove the one real inconsistency, change ch5:260 from "the tier is too small for that to be a precision figure." to "that is must-tier precision as Section~\ref{sec:metrics} defines it, measured on \MustWitnessEdges{} edges from \CensusMustSites{} constructs, which is too few to be a statement about precision in general." This matches the wording of ch7:45-46.

title: ch5 says no too-small scope was found after reporting 4 it refuted
evidence: ch5:609-610: "where the rendered interface could judge it, it was not found to be too small". ch5:593 says the oracle refuted too-small scopes "\ScopeUnpredicted{} times" (=4), and ch1:189 says the section "refutes \ScopeUnpredicted{} of them". ch5:398-406 explains the 4 as an empty scope the running application shows to be non-empty, which is a scope too small.
consequence: The same section concludes the opposite of its own measurement on the limitation the thesis calls its sharpest.
fix: Replace ch5:609-610 with: "...and that where the rendered interface could judge it, it was too small \ScopeUnpredicted{} times, each a site attribution left unplaced."

verdict.reasoning:
The contradiction holds, and it sits inside a single paragraph. ch5-results.tex:588-612 is the one paragraph that answers RQ3. At line 593 it says the oracle "can refute a scope that is too small, and did so \ScopeUnpredicted{} times" (generated-probe.tex:89, \ScopeUnpredicted = 4). At lines 609-610 the same paragraph concludes "where the rendered interface could judge it, it was not found to be too small". The built PDF prints the same claim (thesis.txt:3297-3298). ch1-introduction.tex:189 also says Section sec:res-scope "refutes \ScopeUnpredicted{} of them", where "them" means scopes that are too small. ch5:403-404 says "attribution computed the empty scope", and ch5:406 says the running application "shows [it] to be non-empty". An empty scope that should be non-empty is a scope that is too small, so the four are attribution outcomes the oracle judged too small.

The best defence is that the authors mean computed scopes only. ch5:389 says "computed scopes are not too small", and ch6:195-196 and ch7:166-167 call the four sites "attribution declined to place rather than sites it placed wrongly". That reading does not save line 610. Its subject is "it", meaning attribution, and the sentence drops the "computed" qualifier. It also conflicts with line 593's wording in the same paragraph, and line 593 has no such qualifier either. The measurement itself is disclosed (ch5:398-406), so this is a wording error, not a wrong number. It is still a summary sentence that states the opposite of the count given 17 lines earlier.

One part of the finding overreaches. Its "consequence" ties this to "the limitation the thesis calls its sharpest", but ch5:611-612 names the sharpest limitation as scopes being too large, not too small.
verdict.checkedEvidence:
These sources were checked:
- **ch5-results.tex:593:** "too small, and did so \ScopeUnpredicted{} times"
- **ch5-results.tex:609-610:** "where the rendered interface could judge it, it was not found to be too small"
- **ch5-results.tex:398-406:** "attribution computed the empty scope for it", "a scope the analysis declined to compute, which the running application then shows to be non-empty"
- **ch5-results.tex:389:** "computed scopes are not too small on what could be observed"
- **ch1-introduction.tex:188-189:** "a scope that is too small can be refuted ... Section~\ref{sec:res-scope} refutes \ScopeUnpredicted{} of them"
- **ch6-discussion.tex:194-196 and ch7-conclusion.tex:166-167:** both frame the four as "declined to place"
- **generated-probe.tex:85, 86, 89:** \ScopePairs=33, \ScopeConfirmed=29, \ScopeUnpredicted=4
- **thesis.txt:3297-3298:** the PDF prints "was not found to be too small"
verdict.betterFix: Replace ch5-results.tex:609-610, "and that where the rendered interface could judge it, it was not found to be too small.", with: "and that where the rendered interface could judge it, the only scopes it showed to be too small were the \ScopeUnpredicted{} attribution left empty, at sites it declined to place." This keeps line 593 ("did so \ScopeUnpredicted{} times") and ch1:189 true, and matches the framing at ch5:406, ch6:195-196 and ch7:166-167. If the authors instead want the claim limited to non-empty scopes, they should change line 593 at the same time, for example to "and did so \ScopeUnpredicted{} times, each a scope attribution left empty". Otherwise the paragraph still contradicts itself.

title: The 11/11 guard-removal result uses a criterion loosened after removals scored as wrong
evidence: ch4:479-481 says the ninth and tenth corrections "followed a change in the extractor rather than a figure". The text then says the old rule "scored such a removal as wrong", which is a figure. The criterion became "detected when some edge loses a guard it carried", plus a new exclusion. generated-rq4.tex then gives \MutGuardDetected=11 of \MutGuardScored=11, with \MutExcludedGuard=6 excluded. ch7:65-67 and ch6:97-98 report 11/11 without saying the scoring rule changed after the outcome.
consequence: A perfect score on the operator the thesis says the corrections were about is reported in the conclusion without saying its success criterion was redefined after a disappointing score.
fix: ch7:65: "Removing a guard is detected in \MutGuardDetected{} of \MutGuardScored{} scored mutants under the criterion adopted after the router-guard change (some edge loses a guard it carried; Section 4.x)." ch4:480: replace "rather than a figure" with "and were found when removals began to score as wrong".

verdict.reasoning:
The overclaim does not hold up. The finding says the perfect guard score is reported in the conclusion without noting that the scoring rule was redefined after a removal scored as wrong. Four things the record shows:

(1) The change is disclosed where the method and the result are reported. ch4-evaluation.tex:482-492 lists both changes among the numbered corrections. It says the old rule "scored such a removal as wrong" and gives the new criterion and the new exclusion. ch5-results.tex:738-740 states the criterion next to the figure: "\MutGuardDetected{} of \MutGuardScored{} ... each judged by whether some edge loses a guard it carried". Not repeating that criterion in the summaries at ch6:97-98 and ch7:59-60 is ordinary summary practice. It does not hide anything.

(2) The new exclusion played no part in the score. generated-rq4.tex:88 sets \MutExcludedUncarried=0. The 6 exclusions (\MutExcludedGuard) are \MutExcludedUnreached=5 plus \MutExcludedNoScreen=1 (generated-rq4.tex:85-87), and both of those rules already existed in harness 1.5.0. Linking the 6 exclusions to the new rule, as the finding does, is wrong.

(3) The 11/11 does not depend on the change. Harness 1.5.0 detected a removal when the guard changed on SOME edge entering a reached screen of the guarded route: `d.guardChanged.some(c => reached.some(rt => c.includes('-> '+rt+':')))`, in the old check removed by 563880d. In results-rq4/rq4-*-attributed.json, every one of the 11 DETECTED REMOVE_GUARD mutants has a guardChanged edge into a screen of its own guarded route. Examples: realworld `/article/:slug -> /editor/:slug` and `-> /login`; bitwarden oss-routing:684 (the UserLayout parent) `-> /settings/account`; organization-settings:17 `-> .../settings/policies`; alfresco aca-content.routes.ts:111 `o_UserInfoComponent -> /profile`, where profile is a child of that empty-path route (corpus file, lines 108-116). So the original criterion would also have scored 11/11 on the reported attributed run. The new criterion is also stricter in one respect: a guard must be lost, not merely changed.

(4) Both changes were triggered by single WRONG verdicts, not by a weak headline figure. The 1.5.0 WRONG that prompted 1.6.0 came from alfresco WITHOUT attribution (mutate.mjs 1.6.0 header), not from the attributed figure. The 1.7.0 change fixes a set-comparison bug that 1.6.0 itself introduced, and it restores the verdict 1.5.0 would have given.

The concern is therefore unfounded: the success criterion was not quietly loosened to rescue a disappointing headline. A smaller, separate wording issue does exist at ch4:482-486:
- "both followed a change in the extractor rather than a figure" is not true of the tenth change. That one fixes a harness bug and followed no extractor change. Its own header (mutate.mjs 1.7.0) says it was found because 1.6.0 "scored WRONG".
- "must change every edge entering the guarded screens" misdescribes the 1.5.0 rule, which required a change on some such edge, not every one.

That issue is minor and different from the claimed major overclaim.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds. ch6-discussion.tex:97-98 says guard removal "is the operator the earlier state of this extractor was weakest on". That ranks the earlier instrument's operators against each other, and the thesis twice says it cannot make that comparison. ch5-results.tex:656-657 says "Which operator moved furthest cannot be said, since no per-operator mutation result from the earlier instrument survives to compare against". ch5-results.tex:741-742 says "no per-operator figure from the earlier instrument survives to put a number on the movement". - CHANGE_NAV_TARGET: 12 detected, 1 missed, 4 wrong, so 12/17 (71%).

title: RQ4 conclusions generalise from three mutated applications to the graph in general
evidence: ch7:52: "The answer to RQ4 is that the graph is sensitive to authored source changes in the constructs it represents". ch7:107-108: "a change to it is almost always visible in the graph". These rest on realworld, alfresco and bitwarden only, with \MutSampled=70 of \MutCandidates=249 and a quota of 8. mifos, which holds \RoundTwoMifosShare=75.6% of in-scope sites, and ghostfolio and k8sdash were not mutated. "bitwarden, which has the highest guard density in the corpus" is typed by hand with no generated figure. A rough grep (ASSUMPTION-level) finds 61 guard properties over 135 path entries in ghostfolio/apps/client/src against 83 over 211 in bitwarden/apps/web/src.
consequence: A property measured on three applications is stated as a property of the graph. One justification for choosing bitwarden is unmeasured.

- ch7:107-108 widens it further: "Where a construct is in the graph, a change to it is almost always visible in the graph".

- The other chapters do scope it: the abstract (thesis.tex:140, "Mutation testing on three of the applications"), ch5:662 ("three of the six applications") and ch6:94 and 135 ("the other three applications were not mutated"). The overclaim is therefore limited to Chapter 7. ch5:782-783 sits inside a section already scoped at ch5:662, so that citation does not hold.
- Sample sizes are as stated: `\MutCandidates`=249 and `\MutSampled`=70 (generated-rq4.tex:31, 59). ch5:666 gives the quota of eight.
- `\RoundTwoMifosShare`=75.6% exists (generated-round2.tex:93). It is not used in any chapter, and I did not verify its meaning ("in-scope sites"), so that part of the finding is an ASSUMPTION.

(2) "Highest guard density" is typed by hand and backed by no measurement.

title: Two competing causes are given for the 150-edge tier, with no counterfactual measured
where: thesis.tex:119-121, 164-165; ch7-conclusion.tex:144-146 versus ch7-conclusion.tex:43-46, ch6-discussion.tex:77-78, ch5-results.tex:248-251
evidence: thesis.tex:119-121 and ch7:144-146 say the router-guard reading "is where most of the current tier comes from". ch7:43-46, ch6:77-78 and ch5:248-251 attribute the 17-to-150 difference to attribution of shell links. \CensusMustKdash=125 needs both, since \CensusBaseMustKdash=0. No generated macro counts the tier under the superseded rule that gated an edge on every destination guard.
consequence: Both explanations are stated causally, and neither is backed by a recorded counterfactual.
fix: Add a measurement of the tier under the superseded guard rule, or say: "the k8sdash edges need both the shell attribution and the router-guard rule; their separate contributions are not measured".

verdict.reasoning:
Refuted. The finding calls these two "competing causes", but they answer two different counterfactual questions, and they do not conflict.

(B) is the claim at ch7-conclusion.tex:43-46, ch6-discussion.tex:77-78 and ch5-results.tex:248-251. It compares the graph with and without attribution under the same instrument. That counterfactual is recorded in generated macros:
- \CensusBaseMust=17 against \CensusMust=150.
- k8sdash: \CensusBaseMustKdash=0 against \CensusMustKdash=125.
- realworld: \CensusBaseMustRealworld=1 against \CensusMustRealworld=9.
- mifos is 15 in both runs, and bitwarden is 1 in both.
The finding says neither cause has a recorded counterfactual. That is false for (B).

(A) is the claim at thesis.tex:119-121 and 164-165 and at ch7-conclusion.tex:144-146. It compares the router-guard rule with the superseded rule, which gated an edge on every guard its destination carries. It is true that no generated macro counts the tier under the superseded rule. A git-history comparison would not supply one either: the census moved from 9 at fd7b289 to 150 at 0027017, but that range also contains the call-graph commit 22dd294 and the provider-binding commit be43840, and a8c7480 itself changed redirect, comment-blanking and HostListener handling as well as the guard rule.

The counterfactual does not need a re-run, though. It follows from the superseded rule's definition plus the per-construct readings recorded in results-must/tier-reading.json. Every k8sdash, mifos and bitwarden construct is recorded under a guarded parent level that the navigation does not run again:
- k8sdash: the chrome '' route carries AuthGuard.
- mifos: the withShell level carries AuthenticationGuard.
- bitwarden: UserLayoutComponent's '' route carries authGuard and deepLinkGuard.
A rule that gated on every guard of the destination would therefore demote all of them. That covers \CensusMustKdash + \CensusMustMifos + \CensusMustBitwarden = 141 of \CensusMust = 150. The 9 realworld edges have no guard, so they stay either way.

The abstract's wording ("where most of the current tier lies", thesis.tex:120; "mostly", thesis.tex:164) describes what the tier is made of, and the per-app macros plus tier-reading.json support it. ch5-results.tex:1077-1088 gives the same split by application, using macros.

The 125 k8sdash edges do need both the shell attribution and the guard rule. But no passage says either cause is sufficient on its own, so there is nothing contradictory to fix. The most this could be is a clarity nit: ch7:144-146 says "comes from" while the evidence is a hand reading file rather than a generated macro. Since "most" is not a hand-typed figure, that does not break the macro rule.

title: Smaller Angular and validity inaccuracies
evidence: ch2:398-399 says lazy children are in a file "resolved when the application is built". In fact loadChildren runs at run time when the route is first matched. ch2:399-401 lists only canActivate, canMatch and canDeactivate, while the analysis reads canActivateChild, canLoad and resolvers. ch3:155 and ch5:1032 say canLoad runs on every level a navigation enters, but Angular runs it only on the first load of the lazy module, not when it is already loaded or preloaded. This is conservative but not "the way the router decides it" (ch3:151). ch6:230 calls every conversion ratio "a lower bound", yet the next paragraph (ch6:233-) says the denominator also under-counts, and the numerator rests on unverified must rules.
consequence: Background and threat statements contain small factual errors and one non sequitur.
fix: ch2:399: "...defined in another file that the router loads when the route is first matched". Add canActivateChild, canLoad and resolvers to the ch2 list. ch3:155: note "canLoad, which the router runs only on the first load, is taken to run on every entry as a precaution". ch6:230: replace "is therefore a lower bound" with "is biased downward by these two effects and in an unknown direction by the under-count below".

verdict.reasoning:
Three of the four sub-claims hold. The first one, about build-time resolution, only half holds.

(1) ch2-background.tex:396-398 ("lazily ... in another module or file that is resolved when the application is built"). This is not strictly false. The bundler does resolve the import specifier and emit the chunk at build time. But in a sentence that defines lazy loading, it hides that the router fetches the chunk at run time, when the route is first matched. The same sentence also has an error the finding missed: it says loadComponent puts "the child routes" in another file, but loadComponent loads a component, not child routes. So this is wording, not a hard factual error, plus one real slip.

(2) ch2:399-401 says "namely canActivate, canMatch and canDeactivate". "Namely" presents the list as complete. It leaves out canActivateChild and canLoad, which ch3:155-157, ch5:1031-1033 and the extractor all read (packages/adapter-angular/src/routes.ts:103-105,120-124). ch2 never introduces resolvers or runGuardsAndResolvers either. grep finds only an unrelated "resolvers" at ch2:429, and canActivateChild/canLoad do not appear in ch2 at all. The omission is real. The fix must not call resolvers guards, though.

(3) ch3:153 claims the set of guards a navigation runs "is decided the way the router decides it". ch3:155, ch5:1032 and ch6:605 then say canLoad runs on every level the navigation enters, and the code does exactly that: extract.ts:208 puts entered.flatMap(l => [...l.canActivate, ...l.canLoad]) into the guard set. Angular runs canLoad only when it fetches a loadChildren route's children for the first time. Once the routes are loaded it does not run it again, and it never runs it on a route with eager children. The finding's "or preloaded" part is slightly off, because Angular does not preload routes that have canLoad. The core point stands. Concrete evidence: guards-run.test.ts:33 builds { path: 'lazy', canLoad: [load], children: [...] }, a route with eager children where Angular ignores canLoad, and :65-67 asserts that /login -> /lazy/x is demoted to may. The approximation errs toward demotion, so must-tier soundness is unaffected. But "the way the router decides it" overclaims, and the approximation list at ch6:602-608 admits the reuse rule is too cautious without mentioning canLoad.

(4) ch6:229-231 says "Every reported conversion ratio is therefore a lower bound on the fraction of reachable navigation that the extractor recovers". The very next paragraph, ch6:233-245, says the denominator under-counts and concludes the ratio "is therefore recall against an enumerable syntactic proxy ... not against its navigation". Those two statements contradict each other. The lower-bound argument also needs every must label to be right, because the numerator counts constructs that earn must (ch4-evaluation.tex:104-110,194-196). A false must edge raises the ratio. The two over-counts support only a narrower bound.

None of the fixes needs a number, so there is no macro issue.
verdict.checkedEvidence: ch2-background.tex:390-404 (lazy-loading and guard sentences; PDF text thesis.txt:959-960 matches). grep of ch2 for resolver, runGuardsAndResolvers, canActivateChild and canLoad: only an unrelated hit at :429. ch3-analysis.tex:145-160. ch5-results.tex:1025-1036. ch6-discussion.tex:220-262 and 600-608. ch4-evaluation.tex:104-115 and 192-200 (definition of the conversion-ratio numerator). packages/adapter-angular/src/extract.ts:192-213 (runningGuards puts canLoad on every entered level). routes.ts:85-124 (RouteLevel reads canLoad, canActivateChild and resolve). guards-run.test.ts:33 and 65-67 (canLoad on a route with eager children asserted to demote). Angular router semantics, from my knowledge rather than files: getChildConfig runs canLoad guards only when loadChildren is set and _loadedRoutes is undefined, and the preloader skips routes that have canLoad.
verdict.betterFix:
ch2-background.tex:396-401, replace from "Routes can be loaded lazily" through "representing a redirect." with: "Routes can be loaded lazily: \texttt{loadChildren} names another module or file that declares the child routes, and \texttt{loadComponent} another file that declares the component. The bundler resolves that file when the application is built, and the router fetches it when a navigation first matches the route. Routes may also have guards, namely \texttt{canMatch}, \texttt{canLoad}, \texttt{canActivate}, \texttt{canActivateChild} and \texttt{canDeactivate}, which are functions or injectable classes that return either a boolean or a \texttt{UrlTree} representing a redirect, and resolvers, which fetch data the router awaits before it activates the route; \texttt{runGuardsAndResolvers} decides when a route the navigation keeps runs them again."

ch3-analysis.tex:153, replace "which guards a navigation runs is decided the way the router decides it." with: "which guards a navigation runs is decided the way the router decides it, with one exception: \texttt{canLoad} is taken to run on every route the navigation enters, though the router runs it only before a lazy route's children are first loaded, an over-approximation that can only demote."

ch5-results.tex:1032, after "\texttt{canActivate}, \texttt{canLoad} and the resolvers on the levels it enters" insert: "(\texttt{canLoad} on every entry, although the router runs it only on a lazy route's first load)".

ch6-discussion.tex:608, after "makes too cautious." add: "\texttt{canLoad} is likewise taken to run on every entry, though the router runs it only before a lazy route's children are first loaded and never on a route whose children are eager."

ch6-discussion.tex:229-232, replace "Every reported conversion ratio is therefore a lower bound on the fraction of reachable navigation that the extractor recovers, and the true figure cannot be computed without deciding reachability for each construct by hand." with: "These two effects push every reported conversion ratio below the fraction of the parser's reachable constructs that the extractor converts, provided every must label is right. Because of the under-count described next, the ratio is not a bound on the application's navigation as a whole, and the true figure cannot be computed without deciding reachability for each construct by hand."

Separately, the code does not match the prose: the test fixture at packages/adapter-angular/src/guards-run.test.ts:33 calls a route with eager children "lazy". Either give it loadChildren or drop the "lazy" wording.

title: Call graph described as not implemented in Algorithm 1, ch3 complexity section, ch6 future work and Appendix A
evidence: alg-attribution.tex:31 marks the CG loop '\emph{model only}: DI calls, dispatch' and its caption (2-3) says 'model only' loops 'are not implemented in the prototype evaluated in Chapter results' (rendered in thesis.txt:1949). ch3:351-352: 'The part of the analysis that is implemented, the nesting and outlet relations, is the full model with CG and D empty'. ch6:822-826: 'The part of the model that Chapter analysis specifies and the prototype leaves out comes next: the call graph with dependency injection, and the dispatch relations'. appendix-a:212-213: placing a class 'needs the call graph with dependency injection that Section inputs specifies and this implementation does not build'. Against: thesis.tex:107-108 'The prototype implements the first three, the call graph at the granularity of class members'; ch3:468-469 'implements three of the four input relations ... the call graph'; ch6:89-90 'which the current extractor implements'; ch7:70-71; generated-callgraph.tex (CGDirect 7186, CGBound 5536 at 0027017); ablation level 'full' adds AblationFullAddedSites=35.
consequence: Which mechanism the thesis implements, the core of the RQ3 contribution, gets opposite answers. A reader of the algorithm, the only formal statement of the computation, concludes the call graph was never evaluated, which contradicts the abstract and the ablation/GT results it rests on.
fix: alg-attribution.tex:31 comment -> '\Comment{$\mathit{CG}$: member-level, bindings read application-wide; $D$: \emph{model only}}'. ch3:351-352 -> 'The part of the analysis that is implemented, the nesting, outlet and member-level call-graph relations, is the full model with $D$ empty and $\mathit{CG}$ read without the injector hierarchy'. ch6:822-829 -> 'The part of the model the prototype leaves out comes next: the injector hierarchy the call graph ignores, and the dispatch relations that carry NgRx effects and router event subscriptions.' appendix-a:212-213 -> 'because the instrument these reasons were produced on (eb9dab8) predated the member-level call graph; the current extractor places service navigation through it.'

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. The four cited places say the prototype does not implement the call graph. The thesis's own implementation section and code say it does, and the results section evaluates it.

What the thesis says elsewhere, and what the code does:
- ch3-analysis.tex:212-215 lists "the call graph with dependency injection, read at the granularity of class members with bindings taken application-wide" among the parts "implemented in the extractor and ... evaluated in Chapter evaluation".
- ch3:468-470: the pass implements three of the four input relations, including the call graph. Only the dispatch relation is not implemented.
- ch3:502-519 describes the call-graph resolution: declared type, useClass/useExisting bindings, and class hierarchy analysis restricted to the declared type.
- ch5-results.tex:503-515 evaluates it: "the member-level call graph that places a service's navigation" adds \AblationFullAddedSites{} sites (35 in generated-ablation.tex:31).
- thesis.tex:107-108 and ch6:89-91 ("which the current extractor implements") say the same.
- Commit 22dd294 ("feat: attribute a service navigation through a member-level call graph") adds a worklist in callgraph.ts (diff lines 389-399) that joins screen sets along call edges until nothing changes. That is exactly Algorithm 1's Propagate step over CG.

Against this:
- alg-attribution.tex:31 marks the (x,y) ∈ CG ∪ D loop "model only: DI calls, dispatch". Its caption (lines 2-3) says such loops "are not implemented in the prototype evaluated in Chapter results". The built PDF shows the same (thesis.txt line 21 of the algorithm listing).
- ch3:351-352 says the implemented part is "the full model with CG and D empty".
- ch3:353-358 then says the implemented pass "needs no set-valued joins" and costs O(|S|(|C|+|N|)). The finding does not cite this, but it is also false: the call-graph pass is a set-valued worklist.
- ch6:822-826: "the prototype leaves out ... the call graph with dependency injection".
- ch6:826-829 proposes as future work "class hierarchy analysis against Angular's provider declarations". ch3:508-510 says that is what was built.
- appendix-a.tex:212-213: "this implementation does not build" the call graph.

The appendix sentence is defensible only for the instrument the round-two reasons came from. generated-round2.tex was written 2026-10-30. Instrument eb9dab8 is dated 2026-10-30 and is not a descendant of 22dd294 (git merge-base check). The sentence does not say so, unlike ch5:346-350, which qualifies the same fact correctly ("which the instrument these tables measure did not place; the current extractor places ...").

Severity: I rate it major, not critical. No number is wrong. But the algorithm, the formal statement of the computation, and two chapters contradict the abstract on what was implemented and evaluated.

Two problems with the proposed fix:
1. The Appendix A wording types the hash "eb9dab8" by hand, and no macro holds that hash. It also claims the current extractor places these sites, which ch3:531-532 contradicts: "A class the call graph does not reach and nothing injects still has no scope."
2. The ch3 fix leaves the following "no set-valued joins" sentence, which becomes partly false.

A related stale label not in the finding: generated-before-after.tex:26 has the harness row "In a service or guard (not implemented)", produced at eb9dab80. ch5:346-350 explains it, so it is only a label problem.

title: Abstract and ch7 attribute the near-zero must conversion to unevaluated guards; the guard-only counterfactual and the fate data say conditions
evidence: thesis.tex:89-92: 'recovers almost no navigation construct as a deterministic transition ... because the extractor does not evaluate the guards almost every such transition passes'. ch7:24-26: 'That measures what the extractor can prove without evaluating guards, which is little, rather than what the applications do'. verdict.reasoning:
The core of the finding holds; two parts of it overreach.

Holds: thesis.tex:89-92 (PDF line 54) says the extractor recovers almost no construct as deterministic "because the extractor does not evaluate the guards almost every such transition passes". ch7-conclusion.tex:25-27 says the small tier "measures what the extractor can prove without evaluating guards, which is little, rather than what the applications do". The thesis's own counterfactual contradicts both. guard-only.mjs sets UIGRAPH_IGNORE_GUARDS=1, which only switches off the `gated` term in extract.ts:397. Every other may cause in `common` (capMay, viaWildcard, aux, ambiguous, conditional, holes), plus resolves and self-target, still applies. The run counts sites with the same filter as graph-census.mjs mustSiteKeys, `(w.modality ?? 'must') === 'must'`, so GuardOnlySites=66 compares like-for-like with CensusMustSites=25. With every guard passed, 66 of RoundTwoInScope=1777 constructs convert, about 3.7%, which is still "almost no". Guard non-evaluation therefore cannot be why conversion is near zero. The claim that "almost every such transition" passes a guard is also unsupported. Among edges that clear every other rule, GuardOnlyGuarded=41 of GuardOnlyMust=191 carry a guard, and GuardOnlyUnguarded=150 is exactly CensusMust. ch5:1104-1106 itself is more careful: "some of the transitions are there, behind guards". The abstract and ch7 claim more than that.

Overreaches:
(1) The finding's replacement cause, that "almost every such transition runs under a condition", is ASSUMPTION at the population level. MustCtxConditional=32/36 and MustCtxAllConditional=17/20 describe only the citations behind the earlier round's 20 must edges. That is a selected subset which had already cleared the other rules. No macro or result breaks the 1777-66 gap down by demotion reason. That gap includes about 21.7% never recovered (RoundTwoRecovered=78.3%: dynamic 14.5%, unplaced 5.6%). It also includes the attribution cap (capMay in extract.ts, "a cap from attribution" at ch5:1007), which is an extractor approximation, not "what the applications do". So the finding's "a property of the applications" is unsupported too.
(2) The fate data does not "say conditions". With guard taken first, MustFateGuard=10 against MustFateCondition=6. ch5:1024-1025 says either correction alone moves bitwarden's edges.
(3) ch1-introduction.tex:177-180 is not defective. It is about the earlier instruments' tier, it names conditions first and then guards, and it matches MustCtxAllConditional.

The fix should therefore remove the single-cause "because guards" claim and quantify the gap with existing macros, without putting conditions in its place.

verdict.reasoning:
Part of this finding holds up and part does not. What survives is minor.

**The ch5:1114 contradiction claim does not hold.**
- The sentence 'Each correction removed a claim the extractor could not support' is literally true for all four corrections:
  - The first correction removed must edges that the extractor at f17a302 had published without reading the guard. Those claims had no support at the time, even where the navigation does happen.
  - The fourth correction removed 17 of the round's 20 edges (MustFateGuard=10, MustFateSelfLoop=1, MustFateCondition=6).
- The sentence says nothing about corrections only removing claims. Three paragraphs earlier the thesis says plainly that the fourth correction added edges: ch5:1076-1078 'It is not the round's tier made smaller. Reading guards as the router runs them lets through the navigations between screens that share a guarded parent, and that is where most of the tier now is.' ch7 says it again just before the quoted 'each claim ... was withdrawn' line ('that is where most of the current tier comes from ... under one guarded parent').
- The '... cost is paid in RQ1' framing also roughly holds. The round's RQ1 numerator, summed from final7 *.fin.L.json CONVERTED_MUST, is 12+14+2=28 of 1820 (1.5%). After the fourth correction it is CensusMustSites=25.

- The finding's own replacement text is also wrong for k8sdash. It says the fourth correction 'restored' k8sdash's edges, but k8sdash had 0 must edges in the round (RoundTwoMustEdgesMifos/Realworld/Bitwarden = 1/9/10, which sum to 20). Its 125 edges come from attribution (CensusBaseMustKdash=0), so nothing was restored there.

**What survives is in ch6:836-838.**
- The text says reading mifos's wrapper guard 'is what took that application's deterministic tier from an order of magnitude more edges down to \RoundTwoMustEdgesMifos{}' (=1).
- That is true on the round's instrument. On the current extractor the guard accounts for none of mifos's tier. In results-must/guard-only.json, mifos has must=15, unguarded=15, guarded=0: treating every guard as letting the navigation through leaves mifos at 15, the same as CensusMustMifos=15.
- Each of the 19 mifos readings in tier-reading.json places its construct under the withShell level, 'whose AuthenticationGuard does not run again' (the tabs entry says only 'the parent level is shared').

This is a staleness and framing problem in the Discussion chapter, not a contradiction in the results. It is minor.

title: RQ3 precision verdict: ch5 answers positively while ch5 elsewhere and ch7 say there is no precision figure
evidence: ch4:272-273: 'RQ3 is answered positively only if coverage rises and must-tier precision does not fall.' ch5:587: 'Scope attribution therefore raises coverage without lowering must-tier precision, which is what RQ3 asks.' ch5:259-260: '...the tier is too small for that to be a precision figure.' ch7:45-46: 'the tier is too small for that to be a statement about precision in general.' ch6:79-82: on the round instrument the 20/20 clean tier had edges that 'for most of them' did not occur on every input (MustFateKept=2 of 20), so the witness check behind ch5:255-257 is necessary but not sufficient (ch5:995-998).
consequence: The same RQ gets a positive verdict at ch5:587 and an explicit no-verdict at ch5:260 and ch7:45. Under ch4's own criterion, RQ3 cannot be answered positively when no precision figure exists.
fix: ch5:587 -> 'Scope attribution therefore raises coverage, and on the must tier it added edges without adding a witness-check failure; the tier is too small for that to be a precision result, so RQ3's precision half is answered only by the ground truth of Section res-groundtruth, on one application.'

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds in part. Its ch7 leg and its proposed fix do not.

**Where it holds (inside ch5):**
- ch5-results.tex:256-260 reports the current tier (\CensusBaseMust=17 to \CensusMust=150, \MustWitnessViolations=0) and then says "the tier is too small for that to be a precision figure". There is no "in general" or "beyond this corpus" to limit that.
- ch5-results.tex:587-588 then says, without qualification, "Scope attribution therefore raises coverage without lowering must-tier precision, which is what RQ3 asks." So the chapter calls the evidence "not a precision figure" and then gives a positive precision verdict on it.
- The only other precision claim in ch5 is at :255-257 ("precision on the must tier did not fall", 18 to 20 edges, from \AttrMustBefore and \AttrMustAfter). That is the old instrument. ch6-discussion.tex:79-82 says most of those 20 clean edges did not occur on every input. ch5-results.tex:995-998 says the witness check cannot find that kind of error.
- Neither of the three qualifications at ch5:588-612 mentions that the witness check is blind to this.

**Where it does not hold:**
1. ch7-conclusion.tex:45-46 is not an explicit no-verdict. It says "too small for that to be a statement about precision in general". That limits generality, which is compatible with a corpus-level verdict.
2. The positive verdict can be defended by ch4's own operational definition. ch4-evaluation.tex:262-265 defines must-tier precision as the witness-check and route-set pass fraction. On that measure the attributed tier passes all \MustWitnessEdges=150 edges with \MustWitnessViolations=0. A 100% tier cannot be lower than the baseline, so the criterion at ch4:272-273 is met. The defect is the hedge wording at ch5:260 and the missing scope at ch5:587, not a wrong verdict. That is why the severity is minor, not major.
3. The proposed fix confuses two different measures. The ground truth of sec:res-groundtruth (\GTFullPrecision=100.0%, \GTClassPrecision=95.3%) measures the precision of (site, screen) pairs from scope attribution. It does not measure must-tier edge precision, which is what ch4:272-273 makes the RQ3 criterion. Saying RQ3's precision half is answered only by the ground truth would quietly change the criterion.

title: Ch7 RQ2 calls every class confirmed by two independent lines; ch5 says four of five rest on one method plus non-independent observations

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute it. ch7-conclusion.tex:31-33 gives the RQ2 answer as "five defect classes, each confirmed by at least two independent lines of evidence, at least one of them from a named evaluation method", with no qualification. The body says otherwise in three places:

- ch6-discussion.tex:373-378 says the two-line requirement "is a weaker control than it first appears" and that for those four classes "the control is one method plus a judgement I made myself".

I rate it minor rather than major:
1. ch7's wording copies the stated acceptance rule word for word (ch1-introduction.tex:117-120, the tab:defects caption at ch5:106-108, ch7:90-91). ch5:99-100 says all five classes "have at least two confirmations", so by the thesis's own rule the classes are admitted.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds. Two parts of its evidence are wrong, and its proposed fix is wrong.

**What holds**

- **The claim being checked.** ch7-conclusion.tex:105-107 (thesis.txt:5118) says attribution recovers "far fewer on the larger applications, where node defects limit it". `\TabBeforeAfter` (generated-before-after.tex) gives losses recovered (must+may of before):

  - alfresco 4 of 18 (22%)
  - ghostfolio 26 of 72 (36%)
  - k8s dashboard 8 of 56 (14%)
  - bitwarden 15 of 53 (28%)
  - mifos 210 of 234 (90%)
- **Bigger apps do not recover less.** `\TabCoverage` gives the sizes: mifos 605/606, bitwarden 98, ghostfolio 84, k8s 67, alfresco 26. The largest app recovers the most after realworld, both by share and in absolute terms. Recovery does not fall with size.
- **Node defects do not explain the gap.** `\TabRemaining` puts "target screen has no node" at 34 of the 170 still lost (`\AttrRemaining`). That is behind "target fully dynamic" (53) and "owner not reached" (50). The node row is 0 for alfresco and 2 for k8s, so what alfresco and k8s lose is not caused by nodes. It dominates only in ghostfolio (23 of 46).
- **The "node extraction is complete" contrast is wrong.** The sentence implies the other apps lack complete node extraction. But k8s is 100.0% in `\TabCoverage` and is one of the `\ProbeExactApps`=2 apps with "Declared incomplete = no" in `\TabProbe`. Its node extraction is as complete as realworld's, yet it recovers only 14%.

By the loss rules at ch4-evaluation.tex:229-238, "Node missing" belongs to the node branch. So the node classes are not empty, and ch5:318 is a separate error.

title: RQ5 answer drifts from 'defect classes' to 'losses' and contradicts ch5's attribution of conditions, dynamic targets and guard placement to the applications
evidence: ch7:112-113: 'the answer is that almost every loss belongs to the tool'. thesis.tex:150 and ch5:832 say 'Almost every defect class' / 'Every class but one resolved to a construct the extractor could read'. But RoundTwoDynamic=14.5% of in-scope sites have destinations only the run time knows. ch5:925-929 calls k8s's dynamic sites 'a habit of the codebase rather than one place to fix'. ch5:1104-1105: 'where an application puts its guard decides how much of its navigation that is'. MustCtxConditional=32/36 round citations run under conditions in application code.
consequence: The conclusion turns a statement about defect classes into one about losses. That overclaims RQ5 and contradicts the evidence that most of the deterministic shortfall is the applications' conditional or run-time-computed navigation.
fix: ch7:112-113 -> 'the answer is that almost every defect class belongs to the tool, with one instructive exception ...; the losses that remain after the repairs are mostly the applications' own: destinations only the run time knows (\RoundTwoDynamic{} of in-scope sites) and navigation that runs only under a condition.'

verdict.reasoning:
The core drift is real. ch7-conclusion.tex:112-113 answers RQ5 with "almost every loss belongs to the tool, with one instructive exception" (the ghostfolio UrlMatcher). The next sentence (ch7:116) says "Every other defect class", so the claim is really about defect classes, and that is how the abstract (thesis.tex:150, "Almost every defect class") and ch5-results.tex:832 ("Every class but one") put it. Read literally, "loss" contradicts the thesis's own accounting:
- Table tab:loss (generated-tables.tex) lists "Dynamic destination" as an outcome: 158 of 1820 constructs at baseline.
- After the repairs, \RoundTwoDynamic = 14.5% of the \RoundTwoInScope = 1777 in-scope sites still have destinations only the run time knows (generated-round2.tex:63).
- ch1-introduction.tex:166-167 states that run-time targets cannot be determined statically in general.
- ch5-results.tex:928-929 calls k8s dashboard's dynamic sites "a habit of the codebase rather than one place to fix", which places them with the application, not the tool.

So the conclusion says one site belongs to the application, while the thesis itself counts 14.5% of in-scope sites as computed at run time. That is an overclaim in an RQ answer.

Two parts of the finding's evidence fail:
1. \MustCtxConditional (32 of 36) is not evidence of the applications' losses. ch5-results.tex:1006-1011 presents it as a defect in the tool's demotion rules: the tool emitted must for navigation under *ngIf, a branch, an await and so on, and now demotes it. It is a repaired tool defect.
2. Guard placement is shared, not purely the applications'. ch7:151 and ch5:1095-1096 frame the small tier as "what the extractor can prove without evaluating a guard", which is a design choice of the tool. ch5:1104-1105 only adds that where the application puts its guard sets how much navigation that covers.

The finding's proposed fix has two problems:
- It names "navigation that runs only under a condition" as an application loss, which is wrong for the reason in point 1.
- It says the remaining losses are "mostly" the applications'. No macro carries that comparison: it is hand arithmetic on 14.5% dynamic against 5.6% unplaced plus 1.5% unaccounted.

Severity is minor rather than major. The very next sentence names the defect class, the abstract and ch5 state the claim correctly, and the same ch7 paragraph already lists "a destination only the run time knows" as accounted for. One word changes the meaning, and the reader can partly recover it from the context.

title: 'Two blind readings' are presented as corroborating the guard and self-loop fates they never judged; ch7 drops ch5's caveat on the current tier's reading
evidence: thesis.tex:114-119 lists the fates ('under a condition ..., behind a guard the reader had missed, or pointing at the screen already displayed') and then says 'Two blind readings of every construct behind those edges agree with the extractor at \MustReviewAgreeMin{} of the \MustCtxDistinct{}' (30/30). results-must/review.json note: the readings 'do not judge guards, route order, relative bases or self-loops'. ch3:186 scopes the review to 'the condition rules'. verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute all three parts and could not. Each holds against the source, the harness code and the built PDF.

(1) Abstract scope overclaim. thesis.tex:114-117 (PDF lines 77-81) lists the fates, including 'behind a guard the reader had missed' and 'pointing at the screen already displayed'. The next sentence says 'Two blind readings of every construct behind those edges agree with the extractor at 30 of the 30'. That figure comes from route-oracle/must-context.mjs:163. The script counts a construct as agreeing only when `runsAlways !== (c.condition === null)` is false. It compares the condition dimension and nothing else: not guards, not self-loops, not even the destination. The review.json note says the same: the readings 'do not judge guards, route order, relative bases or self-loops'. The guard fate is the largest one (\MustFateGuard=10 of \MustCtxEdges=20), and the self-loop fate (\MustFateSelfLoop=1) is outside the reading too. So the abstract presents the agreement figure as corroborating fates it never tested. Chapter 3 (lines 186-189) scopes the review correctly as 'for the condition rules', so the abstract also contradicts the thesis's own body.

(2) The conclusion drops a caveat. ch7-conclusion.tex:148-150 says the current tier's constructs were 'read against the source' with no qualification. ch5-results.tex:1089-1091 says that reading 'was made once and with the extractor's decisions in view ... not an independent second reading'. The ch7 sentence is literally true but omits a limitation the body states. On its own this part is minor.

(3) 'By hand' contradicts the AI-use declaration. ch5-results.tex:1046 (PDF line 3766) says the readings were 'each made by hand from the sources without the readers'. Four other sources say the assistant made them: ch5:1001-1002 ('the review and the panels were made with the assistant'), ch3:186-187 ('the assistant the declaration describes read the constructs'), the review.json note ('made ... by the AI assistant'), and thesis.tex:185 (the declaration itself). The harness comment at must-context.mjs:154 repeats 'by hand'. Calling AI-made readings 'by hand' in a thesis with a mandatory AI-use declaration is a factual inconsistency, not a matter of style.

Severity is major, not minor, for two reasons: the abstract overstates how far the evidence was independently checked for the largest fate class, and the 'by hand' wording conflicts with the declaration. No number is wrong.

(1) The abstract, thesis.tex:137-138 (PDF thesis.txt:100), says "On the other five applications the sets are checked in one direction only." The other five besides realworld are alfresco, ghostfolio, k8s dashboard, bitwarden and mifos. ghostfolio is checked in no direction:

fix: ch6:97-98 -> 'Removing a guard was detected in every scored mutant of all three; no per-operator result from the earlier instrument survives, so how far this operator moved cannot be said.'

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute the finding and could not. The contradiction is real, but it rests on one sentence and changes no figure.

1. **What ch6 says.** ch6-discussion.tex:97-98 says guard removal is "the operator the earlier state of this extractor was weakest on". That ranks the operators, and placed right after "detected in every scored mutant" it implies guards improved the most.
2. **What ch5 says.** ch5-results.tex:656-657 says "Which operator moved furthest cannot be said, since no per-operator mutation result from the earlier instrument survives". ch5-results.tex:741-742 repeats that no per-operator figure survives.
3. **What ch4 requires.** ch4-evaluation.tex:398-400 says any comparison resting on an earlier state of the extractor must name the commit and take its figures from that commit's generated results. The ch6 sentence names no commit and cites no figure.
4. **No result file backs the ranking.** The route-oracle results-* directories hold no earlier per-operator mutation result. results-rq4 has only the current attributed and baseline JSON files. results-must/mutation-sweep.json is the demotion-rule sweep, a different experiment.
5. **The sentence is not new.** git log -S shows it and both ch5 caveats were added together in d1bb48c, not in 3ebbf35, so the author wrote the contradiction in one pass.

**The best defence, and why it falls short.** ch5:648-650 does say the earlier extractor could not detect guard mutants on routes returned by a wrapper function. So "guards were a weak spot" is supported in words. "Weakest" is not:
- Retargeting was also broken earlier, by the harness defect at ch5:651-655.
- No earlier figure for routerLink deletion survives.
- The ranking would need exactly the per-operator data ch5 says is gone.

**Why minor, not major.** It is one sentence of discussion prose. The macro values it sits beside are right: MutGuardDetected=11 of MutGuardScored=11 in generated-*.tex, so "every scored mutant" holds. No conclusion depends on the ranking. An examiner would still notice the claim contradicting ch5's own stated limit.

title: Protocol correction count: 'Eight' in ch4 and ch6, 'ten' two paragraphs later in ch4 and in ch7

  2. witness check

  8. guard exclusion rule
  9. removed-guard judgment

title: Call graph said to 'replace' the class join that the ground truth convicted, while that join still runs as the fallback

Every remaining target (`rest`) gets `scopes.serviceScreens.get(f)`, which is the per-class injector join built in attribute.ts:374-388. The problem is imprecise summary wording and an unmeasured fallback, not a hidden defect.

title: Abstract and ch5 say the fourth correction keeps 2 of the round's 20 edges; ch5 says a third, the joined edge, stays must
evidence: thesis.tex:162-164: 'of its must edges ... all but \MustFateKept{} (2) run only once something has happened ...'. ch5:943,948: 'keeps \MustFateKept{} of the tier's edges'. ch5:1069-1071: '\MustFateJoined{} (1) is joined: its own construct earns may, and the edge stays must because the shell's logo links ... yield it too'. must-context.json: realworld '/profile/:username/favorites -> /' fate 'joined'. CensusMustRealworld=9 includes it.
consequence: The survivor count of the round's tier is 3 edges, not 2, by ch5's own account.
fix: thesis.tex:162-164 -> 'all but \MustFateKept{} keep no construct that earns must; one more stays must only because the shell's logo links now yield it.' Make the same change in the ch5:943/948 captions.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The finding holds for the ch5 sentence and the ch5 caption, and partly for the abstract.

**Macro values** (generated-must.tex:3,11-15): MustCtxEdges=20, MustFateKept=2, MustFateJoined=1, MustFateGuard=10, MustFateSelfLoop=1, MustFateCondition=6. These add up to 20, and the joined edge sits in its own bucket.

**The joined edge** (route-oracle/results-must/must-context.json): it is realworld '/profile/:username/favorites -> /', fate "joined", sites 1, unconditionalSites 0. So its own construct is conditional.

**ch5 says it stays must.** ch5-results.tex:1069-1071 says this edge "stays must because the shell's logo links, now drawn per screen, yield it too". Drawing the shell edges per screen is part of the fourth correction itself (ch5:1039-1041).

**The census agrees.** results-census/census.json gives realworld 10 screens and must 9, which is CensusMustRealworld=9. These are the logo-link edges from the 9 non-root screens into /, and /profile/:username/favorites is one of them.

**So 3 of the round's 20 edges are still must** (2 kept + 1 joined), and 17 are demoted (10 guard + 1 self-loop + 6 condition).

**Where the prose is wrong:**
- **ch5:943 and the ch5:948 caption** say the fourth correction "keeps \MustFateKept{} of the tier's edges". The PDF renders this as "keeps 2 of the tier's edges" (thesis.txt:3642, 3672). That contradicts ch5:1069-1071, where a third edge is held at must by the same correction.
- **thesis.tex:162-164 (abstract).** "all but 2 run only once something has happened, behind a guard, or to the screen already displayed" is technically true of the joined edge's own cited construct. But its subject is edges. Read with "Little of the round's deterministic tier survived", it tells the reader 2 edges survived and that the joined edge runs only conditionally. ch5 says that edge is must, which means it occurs on every execution.

**Already correct:** thesis.tex:115 and ch7-conclusion.tex:139 use the precise wording "keeps a construct that earns must in \MustFateKept{}", so the fix can reuse that wording.

**Problem with the finding's own fix:** it hand-types "one more". That should be \MustFateJoined{}.
verdict.checkedEvidence:
- **generated-must.tex:3,11-16:** MustCtxEdges 20, MustFateKept 2, MustFateJoined 1, MustFateGuard 10, MustFateSelfLoop 1, MustFateCondition 6, MustFateRetargeted 0.
- **generated-census.tex:26,38:** CensusMust 150, CensusMustRealworld 9.

- **results-census/census.json:** realworld has screens 10 and must 9.
- **thesis.tex:162-164** and **ch5-results.tex:943,948** use \MustFateKept{} as the count of survivors.
- **ch5-results.tex:1039-1041:** the shell edge is drawn per screen under the fourth correction.
- **ch5-results.tex:1065-1071:** gives the fate breakdown and says the joined edge stays must.
- **Precise wording to reuse:** thesis.tex:115 and ch7-conclusion.tex:139 ("keeps a construct that earns must in \MustFateKept{}").
- **PDF text (thesis.txt):** line 126 "all but 2"; lines 3642 and 3672 "keeps 2 of the tier's edges".
verdict.betterFix:
ch5-results.tex:943-944: "A fourth correction, made after the table was measured, keeps a construct that earns must in \MustFateKept{} of the tier's edges, holds \MustFateJoined{} more at must only through the shell's logo links, and is reported after the first three."

ch5-results.tex:948 (caption): "...and before the fourth correction of this section, which keeps a construct that earns must in \MustFateKept{} of the tier's edges and holds \MustFateJoined{} more at must through the shell's logo links."

thesis.tex:162-164: "Little of the round's deterministic tier survived this scrutiny: of its must edges, which led to the application root and the sign-in screen, only \MustFateKept{} keep a construct that earns must, and \MustFateJoined{} more stays must only because the shell's logo links now yield it; the rest run only once something has happened, behind a guard, or to the screen already displayed."

Check: the rest is 20 - 2 - 1 = 17, which equals MustFateGuard 10 + MustFateSelfLoop 1 + MustFateCondition 6, so the wording matches the macros.

title: RQ1 numerator defined differently in ch1 than in ch4/ch5
evidence: ch1:107-109: 'the fraction of navigation constructs ... witnessed by at least one deterministic (must) transition'. ch4:195-196: 'a construct a must edge cites only as evidence for may does not count'. ch5:1162-1163: 'on the current instrument, constructs that earn must themselves'. generated-census.tex: CensusMustCitedSites=31 vs CensusMustSites=25.
consequence: Under ch1's definition the reported RQ1 figure would be 31, not 25.
fix: ch1:108-109 -> 'the fraction of navigation constructs that earn a deterministic (must) transition on their own, not merely cited by one.'

verdict.reasoning:
Refuted. ch1 does not set up a different definition. It gives the same headline wording that the formal definition uses and points to that definition.

(1) ch1-introduction.tex:99-100 says "The exact measures are defined in Section~\ref{sec:metrics}". That label is at ch4-evaluation.tex:90.

(2) The formal definition at ch4-evaluation.tex:104-105 opens with the same phrase ch1 uses: "the fraction of navigation constructs that are witnessed by at least one must edge". ch4:108-109 then adds the qualifier: "on the current instrument a construct counts as converted only where it earns must itself". ch5-results.tex:1161-1163 repeats the headline and then the qualifier. So ch1 states the definition in summary and leaves the instrument detail to Chapter 4. The chapters do not conflict.

(3) The claim "Under ch1's definition the reported RQ1 figure would be 31" relies on a reading ch1 does not support. \CensusMustCitedSites=31 (graph-census.mjs:82) counts every witness and merged witness of a must edge. That includes merged witnesses that earn only may on their own (graph-census.mjs:79-80, 88-90). The idea of merged witnesses is not introduced until ch4:106-107. A reader of ch1 cannot read "witnessed by" as "cited as a merged may-witness". The RQ1 question in ch1:102-103 asks how much navigation static analysis can "recover as deterministic transitions". A construct that earns only may is not recovered as deterministic. Read naturally, ch1 gives \CensusMustSites=25, the figure ch5 reports.

At most this is a slight under-specification in an introduction that explicitly defers to the metrics section. It is not an inconsistency between chapters. The proposed fix would also bring the "cited by" / merged-witness distinction into Chapter 1 before the reader has the concept.
verdict.checkedEvidence: ch1-introduction.tex:99-100 ("The exact measures are defined in Section~\ref{sec:metrics}"), 102-103 (RQ1 asks about recovery "as deterministic transitions"), 107-109. ch4-evaluation.tex:90 (\label{sec:metrics}), 104-111 (formal definition: the same "witnessed by at least one must edge" headline plus the "earns must itself" qualifier), 194-196. ch5-results.tex:34-37, 1109-1114, 1161-1163. generated-census.tex:34-35 (CensusMustSites=25, CensusMustCitedSites=31). route-oracle/graph-census.mjs:79-90: mustSites counts witnesses with modality must; mustCitedSites counts every witness and merged witness of a must edge, whatever its own modality. PDF text thesis.txt:384 and :2074 render the same headline phrase in ch1 and ch4.
verdict.betterFix: No change is needed. If the author wants ch1 to read the same as ch4 without bringing in merged witnesses, a minimal edit at ch1-introduction.tex:108-109 would be: "fraction of navigation constructs in the source code that the graph turns into a deterministic (\emph{must}) transition on their own evidence."

title: Ch6 says the coverage gain 'was not bought by widening the must tier' in the sentence that reports the tier widening from 17 to 150
evidence: ch6:75-78: 'No construct that the baseline converted was lost, so the coverage gain was not bought by widening the must tier, and after the fourth correction the tier holds \CensusBaseMust{} (17) edges without attribution and \CensusMust{} (150) with it'.
consequence: The sentence is self-contradictory. The intended claim is about not losing baseline must constructs.
fix: ch6:75 -> 'No construct that the baseline converted was lost, so the coverage gain cost the must tier nothing, and ...'

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the finding. ch6-discussion.tex:75-77 says "the coverage gain was not bought by widening the must tier". The same sentence then says the tier "holds \CensusBaseMust{} edges without attribution and \CensusMust{} with it". Those macros resolve to 17 and 150 in generated-census-base.tex and generated-census.tex, and the built PDF (thesis.txt:4158-4160) shows "17 edges without attribution and 150 with it". So the tier does widen, and attribution is what widens it.

I also checked whether "widening" could mean "loosening the must criterion", which would avoid the contradiction. The thesis does not support that reading:
- ch5-results.tex:252-254 says "the tier grew from \AttrMustBefore{} edges to \AttrMustAfter{}" (18 to 20).
- ch5-results.tex:247-251 says the shell constructs attribution recovers are what add the must edges.
- \AttrRecoveredMust{} = 7 (generated-before-after.tex:53): recovered constructs went onto the must tier.

So part of the coverage gain is the must tier getting wider. The premise "No construct that the baseline converted was lost" (\AttrRegressed{} = 0, generated-before-after.tex:55) shows the gain did not cost the baseline anything. It does not show the tier stayed the same size. The clause contradicts the sentence it sits in and ch5's own wording.

Severity is minor. The supported claim and every number are right; only the inference wording is wrong.

The proposed fix ("cost the must tier nothing") is accurate: \AttrRegressed{} = 0 and \MustWitnessViolations{} = 0. But it removes the words "must tier" just before "the tier holds", which makes that "the tier" harder to follow. A tighter version is below.
verdict.checkedEvidence:
- ch6-discussion.tex:75-77, the sentence itself; the commit diff shows this clause was left as unchanged context in 3ebbf35.
- generated-census-base.tex:26: \CensusBaseMust = 17. \CensusMust = 150 (generated-census.tex). \CensusBaseMustSites = 21, \CensusMustSites = 25.
- generated-before-after.tex: \AttrRecoveredMust = 7 (line 53), \AttrRegressed = 0 (line 55), \AttrMustBefore = 18 (line 59), \AttrMustAfter = 20 (line 60).
- generated-must-witness.tex:4: \MustWitnessViolations = 0.
- ch5-results.tex:245-254: "the attributed run has \CensusMust{} must edges against \CensusBaseMust{}" and "the tier grew from \AttrMustBefore{} edges to \AttrMustAfter{}".
- thesis.txt:4157-4160: the rendered text reads "not bought by widening the must tier ... the tier holds 17 edges without attribution and 150 with it".
verdict.betterFix:
Replace ch6-discussion.tex:75-77 ("No construct that the baseline converted was lost, so the coverage gain was not bought by widening the must tier, and after the fourth correction of Section~\ref{sec:res-round2} the tier holds") with:

"No construct that the baseline converted was lost --- \AttrRegressed{} leave the converted classes --- so the coverage gain cost the baseline nothing. The gain does widen the must tier: after the fourth correction of Section~\ref{sec:res-round2} that tier holds"

Leave the rest of the sentence as it is ("\CensusBaseMust{} edges without attribution and \CensusMust{} with it, the added edges being the links of realworld's and k8sdash's shells ...").

title: Dangling cross-references: services as an application's only remaining loss, and a measurement of the stand-in approximations
evidence: ch6:88-89: service sites 'in another [application] they are the only attribution loss left after the implemented pass had run'. TabRemaining (generated-before-after.tex) has no such application: every application with a non-zero service row also has other reasons (e.g. k8s 5/4/2/37, mifos 1/7/3/13), and realworld's row is all 0. ch3:527-528: the guard and effect stand-ins, 'and Section res-round2 measures what they recover'. ch5:786-1290 (res-round2) contains no such measurement; the ablation (ch5:482-488) only withholds them.
consequence: Two claims point to evidence the cited sections do not contain.
fix: Delete the ch6:88-89 clause or cite the instrument it held on. Change ch3:528 to 'and Section res-ablation withholds them below the full level'.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute both halves and could not. Both claims point to evidence that does not exist on the current instrument.

(1) The ch6 claim fails. ch6-discussion.tex:88-90 says the service sites are, "in another [application]", "the only attribution loss left after the implemented pass had run". \TabRemaining (generated-before-after.tex:25-29) is the only per-application table of losses left after attribution, and it has no such column:
- realworld is 0 in every row.
- alf: unreached 8, service/guard 6.
- gf: 17/4/23/2.
- k8s: 5/4/2/37.
- bw: 19/10/6/1/2.
- mif: 1/7/3/13.

The claim also fails on the narrowest reading, which counts only the two failure rows (unreached owner and service/guard) and drops the "scope found" rows. Every application with a non-zero service row also has a non-zero unreached-owner row. If unreached owners count as correct empty scopes (ch5:347-349), then service/guard is the only real failure in all five applications that have losses, not in one singled-out application.
